title: Work and energy: choose the system, then count the transfers

sources.title: OpenStax: Work, energy, and the work-energy theorem

chapters.title: Work depends on force and displacement
points: Use the angle between force and displacement.
A constant 10 N force through 3 m along its direction does 30 J.
At 60 degrees the same force does 15 J.
chapters.script: Welcome back. Newton's laws helped us find acceleration from forces. Energy gives us another route, especially when a question asks for speed after travelling a distance. Start with a ten newton force pulling a block three metres horizontally. If force and displacement point the same way, the force does thirty joules of work. A joule is one newton metre. Now turn the force through sixty degrees while keeping the displacement horizontal. Only the component along the displacement contributes to work. Ten times cosine sixty degrees is five newtons, and five times three gives fifteen joules. That is why the constant force equation is work equals force times displacement times the cosine of the angle between them. The angle is not automatically the angle to the ground. Identify the actual displacement first. Holding a heavy bag still can feel tiring, but the upward force does zero mechanical work on the stationary bag because its displacement is zero. This definition describes energy transfer to the object; it does not measure how tired a person feels.

chapters.title: Positive, negative and zero work
chapters.formula: Along motion: positive; against motion: negative; perpendicular: zero
points: A horizontal push can do positive work.
Sliding friction on a stationary floor does negative work.
Normal force does zero work during horizontal sliding.
chapters.script: Work can be positive, negative, or zero. The sign tells us how a force contributes to the energy balance. A pull along the displacement does positive work. Kinetic friction on a block sliding across a stationary floor acts opposite the displacement, so it does negative work. On that same horizontal floor, weight and the normal reaction are perpendicular to the displacement and do zero work. They still matter: the normal force may determine the friction. Zero work does not mean an absent force. Think about uniform circular motion. The centripetal force continually changes the direction of velocity, but remains perpendicular to the instantaneous motion. It therefore does no work, and speed stays constant. Here is your check before calculating: name the force, identify the displacement, and decide the angle. Do this separately for every force. Never assume that all contact forces do negative work in every possible situation; the moving surface and the chosen object matter.

chapters.title: Net work changes kinetic energy
points: Add work from every external force on the particle.
50 J net work on a 4 kg particle from rest gives v = 5 m/s.
chapters.script: Kinetic energy is one half times mass times speed squared. It is a scalar, so reversing the direction of motion alone does not change it. If speed doubles, kinetic energy becomes four times as large. The work energy theorem says net work done on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy. Why does that connect to Newton's law? For constant net force along a straight line, combine force equals mass times acceleration with v squared minus u squared equals two a s. Multiplying force by displacement gives one half m times v squared minus u squared. The theorem also holds with changing forces when work is calculated correctly along the path. Try an example. Fifty joules of net work act on a four kilogram particle initially at rest. What speed results? Think before substituting. Fifty equals one half times four times v squared. Therefore v squared is twenty five, and speed is five metres per second. Use net work, not just the work of the most visible force. Zero net work means equal initial and final speeds; it does not guarantee unchanged direction or zero acceleration throughout the journey.

chapters.title: A stopping-distance problem
points: For 2 kg at 10 m/s, initial kinetic energy is 100 J.
Stopping in 5 m requires average resisting force 20 N.
The minus sign describes energy removed from the block.
chapters.script: Let us solve a stopping problem using energy. A two kilogram block slides at ten metres per second and stops after five metres on a rough level floor. Assume friction is the only force doing work. We want the average magnitude of the friction force over this distance. Start with the initial kinetic energy: one half times two times ten squared equals one hundred joules. The final kinetic energy is zero. The change is minus one hundred joules. Friction acts opposite the displacement, so its work is minus F times five. Equating the two gives F equal to twenty newtons. The minus sign belongs to the work, while the requested force magnitude is positive. Pause and ask what would change if the initial speed doubled while mass and friction stayed the same. Initial kinetic energy would be four times larger, so the stopping distance would also be four times larger. This is a useful JEE comparison because you can answer it without calculating a stopping time. State the constant friction assumption when making that comparison.

chapters.title: Gravity, energy and the final checklist
chapters.formula: mgh = (1/2)mv² when falling from rest without drag
points: Use the vertical drop h for work done by gravity.
For h = 10 m and g = 10 m/s², v = sqrt(200), about 14.1 m/s.
With resistance, mechanical energy need not stay constant.
chapters.script: Finally, connect work to a falling object. A half kilogram stone falls ten metres from rest. Use g equal to ten metres per second squared and neglect air resistance. Gravity does positive work because force and displacement point downward. Its work is m g h: one half times ten times ten, or fifty joules. That becomes kinetic energy. Fifty equals one half times one half times v squared, so v squared is two hundred and the speed is approximately fourteen point one metres per second. The mass cancels from the final speed under these assumptions. You can also describe this as gravitational potential energy becoming kinetic energy. Near Earth's surface, a vertical drop h reduces gravitational potential energy by m g h. Mechanical energy stays constant when only conservative forces do work in the model. If friction or drag removes mechanical energy, include that work; total energy is not destroyed, but some becomes thermal energy. Before finishing any energy problem, check the object or system, the forces doing work, the initial and final states, and the signs. These foundations prepare you for later lessons on springs, power, and collisions.

quiz.question: A 10 N force acts at 60 degrees to a 3 m displacement. What work does it do?
quiz.explanation: W = Fd cos(60 degrees) = 10 x 3 x 0.5 = 15 J.

quiz.question: A particle's speed doubles. How does its kinetic energy change?
quiz.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared for the same mass.

quiz.question: 50 J net work accelerates a 4 kg particle from rest. What is its speed?
quiz.explanation: 50 = (1/2) x 4 x v squared, so v squared = 25 and v = 5 m/s.

quiz.question: A 2 kg block at 10 m/s stops in 5 m with friction alone doing work. What is the average friction magnitude?
quiz.explanation: Initial kinetic energy is 100 J. Removing it over 5 m requires an average resisting force of 20 N.

quiz.question: Zero net work over an interval implies which result for a constant-mass particle?
options: Initial and final speeds are equal
quiz.explanation: Net work equals the change in kinetic energy. Equal endpoint kinetic energies imply equal endpoint speeds, not necessarily identical velocities.
